subjective.question: What is communication?
subjective.answer: Communication is a process of sharing, understanding and interpreting the feelings and ideas etc. from one person to another. It is the transfer of information from one person (the sender) to another (the receiver) in such a way that the receiver understands the message in the sense the sender intends.

subjective.question: What are the main elements of a communication process?
subjective.answer: The communication process consists of some elements. They are Sender, Encoding, Message, Channel, Receiver, Decoding, Feedback and Noise. These elements are involved in transferring ideas and information: the sender encodes an idea into a message, sends it through a channel, the receiver decodes it and responds through feedback, while noise may disturb the process at any stage.

subjective.question: What is mass communication?
subjective.answer: Mass communication is the process of transmitting messages to a large number of scattered individuals. Mass communication refers to the process of delivery of message, information or entertainment to the masses or public - that is, communication with a large, heterogeneous and anonymous audience with the help of some technology or medium.

subjective.question: What is the difference between Mass Media Communication and Mass Communication?
subjective.answer: Mass communication is the term which is used to describe the large-scale dissemination of messages. It is generally identified with the transmission of messages which happens through the media, such as radio, television, newspapers, films and advertising. Mass media communication is the term which is used to describe the communication process which uses media technology, such as print and broadcast media, to reach a large audience. In short, mass communication is the overall process, while mass media communication refers specifically to communication carried out through media technologies.

subjective.question: What is the difference between journalism and mass communication?
subjective.answer: Journalism is a part of mass communication. Mass communication is a vast area and deals with all the media technologies such as print, electronic and new media. It is a field of study which deals with the process of communication with a large and diverse audience, while journalism is a process of gathering, writing and reporting news for newspapers, magazines, radio and television. Journalism is thus one applied branch - the news branch - of the wider field of mass communication.

subjective.question: Communication is the life line of human society. Discuss the importance and usage of communication in human life. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: Communication is the process of transmitting a message from a sender to a receiver, where the receiver understands the message in the sense the sender intends. It is an essential element of human life; indeed, it is the life line of human society. Human beings cannot live in isolation - they live in groups, families and societies, and all their social relations are built through communication. From morning to night, almost everything we do involves communication: we ask, answer, order, inform, learn, teach, persuade and entertain through it. Through communication we discover the world around us, develop relations with others, help others, influence them and get influenced by them. Education, trade, government, law, health and religion all run on communication. Knowledge passes from one generation to the next through communication, and it was communication - above all the development of language - that helped mankind explore the world and build civilization. A society without communication cannot survive, because coordination, cooperation and understanding among its members would become impossible. That is why communication is rightly called the life line of human society.

subjective.question: What is meant by a communication model?
subjective.answer: A communication model is a systematic representation of an object or event in idealized and abstract form. Models are communication devices for explaining and describing concepts and describing the structure or process of communication. In simpler words, a model can be defined as any diagrammatic representation or picture of an object or event.

subjective.question: Briefly explain the limitations of communication models.
subjective.answer: Communication models are useful for understanding the process, but they have limitations. First, they over-simplify a very complex human process by reducing it to a few elements and arrows. Second, most models present communication as a static, one-way flow, whereas real communication is dynamic, continuous and interactive. Third, models may lead to premature closure - the reader may stop thinking further, taking the model as the complete truth. Fourth, a model can be confused with reality itself, although it is only an abstract representation of it. Finally, models cannot fully capture the role of context, culture, emotions and meanings, which keep changing from situation to situation.

subjective.question: What is meant by frame of reference in communication?
subjective.answer: Frame of reference is a kind of filter, which is individual and may change in different cultures. It is a system of standards and values, usually implicit, underlying a particular viewpoint or rationale. Frame of reference is the sum of one's experiences, education, understanding, awareness and misconceptions about something. A message is interpreted by the receiver through his own frame of reference, which is why the same message can be understood differently by different people.

subjective.question: Demonstrate linguistic barrier with an example.
subjective.answer: A linguistic barrier arises when the sender and receiver do not share a common language, or when the language used is beyond the understanding of the receiver. For example, if a teacher delivers a lecture in English to students whose mother tongue is Urdu and who have a weak command of English, the students will fail to understand the lecture even though the teacher's message is correct and complete. In the same way, heavy technical jargon used before a layman creates a linguistic barrier, because the words carry no meaning for him.

subjective.question: Explain labeling as a language barrier with the help of an example. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Labeling means attaching common nouns or fixed labels to a group of people, which suggests that all the people in that group are similar in behaviour. Language provides us common nouns, and once a label is attached to a person or group, we stop judging them on their individual merit. For example, statements like 'Scots are stingy people', 'Sheikhs are miser' or 'politicians in Pakistan are corrupt' are labels. Even if a particular Scot is generous or a particular politician is honest, the label forces us to see him through the same fixed image. Labeling therefore blocks fair understanding: the receiver reacts to the label instead of the real person, and communication suffers.

subjective.question: Sometimes language itself becomes an obstacle in effective communication. Explain with the help of an example. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Language becomes an obstacle because words do not carry meaning in themselves; meanings lie in the minds of the people who use them. The same word may mean different things to different people, meanings of words change with time, and faults of language such as labeling, polarization and static meanings distort reality. For example, a concrete word like 'table' is understood by everyone in the same way, but an abstract word like 'justice', 'freedom' or 'democracy' is understood differently by different persons. So even when the same language is spoken, a message can be misunderstood because of the language itself.

subjective.question: What is culture?
subjective.answer: Culture is the sum of the language, beliefs, traditions, norms, values and the symbols of a people. It is the way of life of a particular society or group of people - the shared pattern of thinking, behaviour, attitudes and understanding that binds a community and gives people a coherent sense of who they are, where they belong, what they value and how they act.

subjective.question: How is culture important in the communication process?
subjective.answer: Culture is important in communication because people from different cultures encode and decode messages differently. Cultural differences can cause misunderstanding between people of different cultural backgrounds. People in different cultures have different verbal and nonverbal communication styles; for example, a gesture, colour or act of eye contact that is polite in one culture may be offensive in another. The way people from different cultures relate to time, space and interpersonal relations also influences the communication process. A communicator who understands the culture of his audience can avoid cultural conflict and cultural shock and make his message effective.

subjective.question: What is meant by stereotyping?
subjective.answer: Stereotyping is assigning identical characteristics to any person in a group, regardless of the actual variation among members of that group. It is the fixed, exaggerated and preconceived ideas about a particular social group - based on age, race, ethnicity, gender, occupation and so on. In communication, stereotyping means judging an individual not by his own qualities but by the ready-made image of the group he belongs to.

subjective.question: How do media images of female beauty (stereotyping) become unattainable? Give your own opinion. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: In my opinion, the media - especially advertising, films and magazines - present a very narrow and artificial standard of female beauty: an exceptionally slim figure, flawless skin and perfect features. These images are not real; they are produced through selective casting, heavy makeup, lighting, camera angles and digital retouching. When ordinary women compare themselves with these manufactured images, they find the standard impossible to reach, because even the models themselves do not look like that in real life. This unattainable stereotyping creates dissatisfaction with one's own body, lowers self-esteem and pushes many women towards extreme dieting and eating disorders. The media should instead present natural and diverse images of women so that beauty is not reduced to one fixed, unrealistic stereotype.

subjective.question: What is interpersonal communication? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Interpersonal communication is the exchange of messages between two persons, usually face to face, in which both persons act as sender and receiver and immediate feedback is possible. Through interpersonal communication we discover about ourselves and others, establish relationships, help others and influence them. A conversation between two friends, or a discussion between a teacher and a student, is an example of interpersonal communication.

subjective.question: Discuss briefly the journey of books from handwritten to the printed editions. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: In the earliest times, man wrote on the bark of trees, clay tablets, papyrus and parchment. Books were produced by hand: in the monasteries of Europe, monks copied religious texts in scriptoria, and these handwritten manuscripts - like the lavishly decorated Book of Kells - were rare, slow to produce and very expensive. Paper reached the world from China through Baghdad, where the first paper mill was operated in 794 AD. Block printing also came from China, and in 1041 AD Bi Sheng invented movable type there. The decisive change came around 1440 when Johann Gutenberg, a German goldsmith, developed the printing press with metal movable type and oil-based ink in Europe. Printing could now produce hundreds of identical copies quickly and cheaply. Later developments - the steam press, wood-pulp paper and the Linotype machine - turned the printed book into a mass product, and books moved from the monasteries and the rich into the hands of the common reader.

subjective.question: Why could the manuscripts of the monasteries not really affect life in Europe? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: The manuscripts produced in the monasteries could not affect the general life in Europe for several reasons. They were extremely few in number because each copy was written by hand and took months to complete. They were written in Latin, which the common people could not read. Their content was almost entirely religious, and the copies remained locked inside monasteries and churches, accessible only to the clergy. Being rare and costly, they never reached the ordinary people, so they could not change the thinking or daily life of European society.

subjective.question: How did the printed books affect the people who used to read manuscripts? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Printed books changed the experience of readers completely. Instead of depending on a rare, hand-copied manuscript - in which every copy differed from the other because of copyists' errors - readers could now get many identical, reliable and cheap copies of the same book. Reading was no longer limited to listening to a text read aloud in a group; individuals could own books and read them privately. Readers also got access to secular subjects - science, literature, trade and current affairs - in addition to religious texts, which widened their knowledge and encouraged independent thinking.

subjective.question: How did the revival of ideas spread through print? Discuss. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: During the Renaissance, printing presses reproduced the classic texts of antiquity - the works of Greek and Roman scholars, poets and philosophers - which had survived only in a few manuscripts. Once printed, these ideas travelled quickly to universities, scholars and ordinary readers all over Europe. The revival of classical learning weakened the Church's monopoly over knowledge, encouraged humanism, science and critical thinking, and laid the foundation of the modern age. None of this would have been possible at such speed without print.

subjective.question: How did the printing technique help the scholars in the West greatly to create a mark on the thinking of people?
subjective.answer: Before printing, a scholar's ideas could reach only the few people who could hear him or read his single manuscript. Printing changed this completely: a scholar's work could now be reproduced in hundreds of identical copies and distributed across cities and countries at low cost. Translations into local languages carried these ideas beyond the Latin-reading elite to common readers. New scientific, religious and political ideas therefore spread fast, became standardized, and built public opinion on a large scale. In this way Western scholars - reformers, scientists and humanists - were able to influence the thinking of whole societies and leave a lasting mark on history.

subjective.question: How did print media come to the subcontinent? Discuss. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Print media came to the subcontinent through the foreign rulers. European missionaries first brought the printing press - the Portuguese set up a press in Goa in the sixteenth century to print religious literature. Under the British East India Company, printing expanded to the presidency towns of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay. The first newspaper of the subcontinent, Hickey's Bengal Gazette, appeared in Calcutta in 1780. From English, printing soon spread to Persian, Urdu and the regional languages, and newspapers like Jam-e-Jahan Numa and Partap laid the foundation of the local press, which later played a great role in the freedom struggle.

subjective.question: Write a short note on the development of print media in Bombay. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Bombay, now Mumbai, was surprisingly a late starter in print media. The Bombay Herald came into existence in 1789. A year later, a paper called the Courier started carrying advertisements in Gujarati - an early sign of Bombay's commercial press. The Bombay Gazette, started in 1791, merged with the Bombay Herald the following year, in the first media merger of sorts. Like the Madras Courier, this new entity was recognized as the publication to carry official notifications and advertisements, and Bombay went on to become a leading centre of journalism in western India.

subjective.question: Briefly discuss the development of print media in Madras (Chennai). (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The Madras Courier was started in 1785 in the southern stronghold of Madras, now called Chennai. Its founder, Richard Johnson, was a government printer, and the Courier was designated the purveyor of official information in the Presidency. Madras got its second newspaper in 1791, when Hugh Boyd, the editor of the Courier, quit and founded the Hurkaru; tragically, the paper ceased publication when Boyd died within a year. In 1795 competitors to the Courier emerged with the founding of the Madras Gazette and the India Herald - the latter an 'unauthorised' publication, which led to the deportation of its founder Humphreys. The greatest milestone came in 1878, when The Hindu was founded. It played a vital role in promoting the cause of Indian independence, and today it enjoys the highest circulation in South India and is among the top five national dailies of India.

subjective.question: What do you know about Telex? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Telex was a teleprinter exchange service used for written point-to-point communication before the age of fax and email. Subscribers were connected through a network of teleprinters linked by telegraph/telephone lines. A message typed on the sender's machine was automatically printed on the receiver's machine, so both sides had a written record of the communication. Business houses, government offices and news agencies used telex extensively for fast, documented exchange of messages over long distances.

subjective.question: Mention any five developments which led the telephone to its present status, making it a great facility. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Five major developments raised the telephone to its present status: (1) Graham Bell's magnetic telephone of 1876, itself a modified version of the telegraph, which first carried the human voice over wires, despite early voice distortions. (2) Improved microphones and receivers, which made speech clear and loud enough for practical use. (3) Telephone exchanges and switchboards, which allowed any subscriber to be connected to any other instead of needing a separate wire for every pair. (4) Automatic dialling and long-distance (trunk) lines, which removed the dependence on manual operators and linked cities and countries. (5) Electronic and digital exchanges, followed by mobile and cellular telephony, which freed the telephone from fixed wires and turned it into a personal, worldwide facility.

subjective.question: How did the growth of understanding of monetary and fiscal matters change people's economic ideas? Give your own analysis. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: In my analysis, print was the real engine of this change. When the Church's control over written communication broke down and newspapers and periodicals began to involve more people in print communication, money-generation methods and increasing trade became common topics of discussion. As more people came to understand monetary and fiscal matters - how money circulates, how taxes and trade work - economic activity grew and people began to think in practical, material terms rather than purely religious ones. This growth of economies weakened the forces of religion in the West, and society continued to bend towards a material world. Print thus turned economic knowledge from the secret of a few merchants and rulers into a shared public understanding.

subjective.question: What are the major fields of mass communication?
subjective.answer: The major fields of mass communication are: journalism (newspapers, magazines, radio, television and online news), advertising, public relations, broadcasting (radio and television), film and cinema, book and magazine publishing, photography, and the new digital media. All these fields use media technologies to deliver messages to large, scattered audiences.

subjective.question: What is the difference between a newspaper and a magazine? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: A newspaper is published daily (or at short intervals) and mainly carries the latest news of the day - politics, crime, sports, business and weather - printed on cheap newsprint with a very short life. A magazine is published weekly, fortnightly or monthly; it carries features, analysis, interviews and in-depth articles, usually on a specialised theme such as fashion, sports, science or current affairs. A magazine is printed on better paper, uses more photographs and colour, costs more, and is kept and read over a longer period, while a newspaper is read once and discarded the same day.

subjective.question: Do you read a newspaper daily? If yes, then why? If no, then why? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Yes, I read a newspaper daily. It keeps me informed about the important events of my country and the world - politics, economy, sports and weather - in one place and at a very low cost. It improves my general knowledge, vocabulary and understanding of current affairs, which is essential for a student. Reading editorials and opinion articles also helps me form my own views on public issues instead of depending only on the brief and often sensational coverage of electronic media.

subjective.question: Why is a message called a commercial product when used for advertising? What is its basic purpose? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: At times the sender uses a message at mass communication scale to garner commercial benefit, and this approach has given rise to an entirely different industry in mass communication - advertising. Such a message is called a commercial product because, like a product, it is deliberately designed, packaged and sold: it is crafted to attract attention, create desire and persuade the audience to buy a good or service. Its basic purpose is to fetch commercial gain for the sender by influencing the buying behaviour of the receivers.

subjective.question: Advertising is often charged with creating a culture of consumerism. Discuss. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The charge has much substance. Advertising does not merely inform; it creates artificial wants by linking products with happiness, beauty, status and success. Through constant repetition on television, print and social media, it persuades people to buy things they do not really need and to judge themselves and others by what they own - the essence of consumerism. It particularly targets children and young people, promotes brand-consciousness, and encourages the use-and-throw habit. On the other hand, defenders argue that advertising also provides useful information, lowers prices through competition and finances the media. On balance, however, its persuasive design and huge scale do push society towards a culture of consumption in which material goods become the measure of a good life.

subjective.question: How does media present assumptions as reality? Discuss. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The media present assumptions as reality in several ways. First, through selection: by choosing which events and aspects to show, the media make their own version of events appear to be the whole truth. Second, through repetition: an assumption repeated again and again in news, dramas and advertisements begins to be accepted as a fact. Third, through stereotyped portrayals - for example, of women, minorities or professions - which audiences take as real pictures of those groups. Fourth, realistic presentation techniques in film and television blur the line between fiction and fact. Since for most people the media are the main source of knowledge about the wider world, these constructed images are accepted as reality, and people act upon them as if they were true.

subjective.question: What is Article 19 of the 1973 Constitution all about? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Article 19 of the Constitution of Pakistan (1973) guarantees the freedom of speech and expression and the freedom of the press. It provides that every citizen shall have the right to freedom of speech and expression, and there shall be freedom of the press, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of the glory of Islam or the integrity, security or defence of Pakistan or any part thereof, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court or commission of or incitement to an offence.

subjective.question: Write any five codes of ethics which journalists should keep in mind. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Five basic codes of ethics for journalists are: (1) Truth and accuracy - report facts honestly, verify information before publishing and correct errors promptly. (2) Fairness and impartiality - give all sides of a story a fair hearing and do not let personal opinion distort the news. (3) Independence - do not accept bribes, gifts or favours that could influence coverage. (4) Respect for privacy and human dignity - avoid unnecessary harm, be careful with victims of crime and tragedy, and do not publish material that spreads hatred. (5) Accountability and source protection - take responsibility for published work and protect the identity of confidential sources.

subjective.question: How are Public Relations and Advertising taken as forms of mass communication?
subjective.answer: Public Relations and Advertising are taken as forms of mass communication because both use mass media channels - newspapers, magazines, radio, television and the internet - to deliver planned messages to large, scattered audiences. Advertising presents a message about a product, service or brand through paid media space or time in order to persuade the audience. Public Relations presents messages about an organisation, person or cause through media coverage in order to build a favourable image and goodwill. In both cases a sender communicates with the masses through media technology, which is the defining feature of mass communication.
